pages.text:
# Computer networks
 
A packet is a small unit of data sent across a network. It carries part of a message and
enough addressing information for the network to forward it. A long message can travel as
many packets, which the receiving application ultimately reads as a complete exchange.
 
## Local networks
 
A switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network. It learns which devices are
reachable through its ports by observing their hardware addresses. A wireless access point
connects devices over radio and can bridge them to the wired local network.
 
## Routing
 
A router forwards packets between networks. It reads the destination IP address and uses a
routing table to choose a next hop. The next hop may be the receiving device on a directly
connected network or another router farther along the path.

## DNS and addresses
 
DNS resolves names to records, such as an IP address for a host. An application can ask a
resolver for an address before it connects. Resolvers can cache answers until the record’s
time to live expires. DNS lookup and packet forwarding are separate operations.
 
## TCP and UDP
 
TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream. It tracks delivery and can send missing data
again. UDP sends datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees. An application
that needs those properties over UDP has to implement them itself or use a protocol that
provides them.
 
## Latency and bandwidth
 
Latency is how long an operation takes to complete. Bandwidth is how much data a connection
can carry per unit of time. A connection can carry a lot of data while still taking a long
time to deliver a request and its first response.
